sm: The program opens with headlines. Senate Democrats vow to investigate after President Trump pressed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, who had resigned after admitting an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Chuck Schumer promised a probe, and Senator Chris Van Hollen alleged political favors, citing a donation to the White House ballroom without offering evidence. Huang will answer questions behind closed doors from three House committees next week. The Democratic National Committee plans twelve presidential debates starting in June, with a pledge to reject super PAC ads. Other stories cover Florida flooding with nearly five hundred rescues, a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, a new European Union sanctions package, and a deadly candy factory fire in Indonesia with at least twenty-four dead.

Nick Eicher interviews French anthropologist Florence Bergeaud-Blackler about her report on the Muslim Brotherhood. She distinguishes violent jihadism from what she calls Brotherism, a legalist branch of political Islam that seeks to Islamify society gradually without physical violence. She cites changes in France over thirty years, including a 2023 finding that fifty-eight percent of young Muslims there preferred Sharia law to Republican law. She says the movement is flexible, avoids forming its own parties in France, and works through leftist parties, which she compares to a cuckoo placing eggs in another bird's nest. She names the Council on American Islamic Relations and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani as warning signs in the United States.

Bergeaud-Blackler says policy options are limited because the activities are legal, so the response must be education about how the strategy works, and that critics are often accused of Islamophobia. The program then turns to measles. The United States lost its elimination status after twelve months of continuous spread, with nearly six thousand cases this year and hotspots in Pennsylvania, Utah and South Carolina. A woman recalls having measles in 1953. Experts say about one in a thousand cases brings brain swelling, one to three in a thousand die, and one patient infects twelve to eighteen people. Two vaccine doses are ninety-seven percent effective, and hotspots match areas with vaccination rates under ninety-five percent. The story then begins on three Amish schools in New York facing penalties over vaccine rules.

New York ended religious vaccine exemptions after the 2018 and 2019 measles outbreak, and imposed one hundred eighteen thousand dollars in penalties on three Amish schools, with fines up to two thousand dollars per student per day. The state says its law applies equally and protects vulnerable children. Attorney Aaron Siri says the Amish seek only religious accommodation, noting forty-five states allow exemptions, and cites Wisconsin v. Yoder and Mahmoud v. Taylor. The Second Circuit again ruled against them, and the Amish have petitioned the Supreme Court, with New York's response due December second. A short item notes a thirty dollar painting at an estate sale turned out to be by Gertrude Abercrombie and sold for over 1.35 million dollars. A report on the Columbus Zoo and the show Secrets of the Zoo begins.

The zoo story continues with veterinarian Dr. Priya Bapodra and staff describing how the Nat Geo Wild show raised the zoo's profile and still draws visitors. They discuss Stubby the manatee, who helps rescued orphan manatees learn to swim and eat before release, and a sloth bear waking during surgery. The head of animal care says the show influenced how he designs habitats so animals' needs and interactions are visible to the public. Then commentator Cal Thomas criticizes Grand Theft Auto 6, which took in 3.79 billion dollars in first-day sales, citing its sexual content and violence and asking parents whether they know what games their kids play. The program ends with a preview of tomorrow's show and a Bible verse.
